items.title: Cerebras launches CS-4 wafer-scale AI system with up to 30x faster inference than GPUs and modular design for hyperscale deployment [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Cerebras CS-4
items.summary:
Cerebras has introduced the CS-4, a new wafer-scale AI system that delivers up to 30 times faster inference compared to GPU systems, targeting hyperscale data centers. The CS-4 features three WSE-3 Turbo wafers per system, enhanced power delivery, cooling, and I/O, and a modular Nexus Platform Architecture designed to simplify manufacturing, deployment, and upgrades.

The system achieves higher throughput per watt and reduces wafer-to-wafer interconnect latency to 2 microseconds, enabling interactive performance on models exceeding 10 trillion parameters. Its modular compute backpack design integrates power conversion, cooling, and control electronics into a compact package, reducing deployment time from days to hours. The first CS-4 shipments are expected to begin this quarter.

items.title: INXM launches local Rust desktop app using LLM as compiler to create deterministic AI workflows without runtime improvisation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: INXM // local` OSS for using LLM as compiler and not as runtime
items.summary:
INXM has released a local-first Rust desktop application that uses large language models (LLMs) as compilers rather than runtime engines, enabling users to describe intent in chat which is then compiled into typed, validated plans executed deterministically. The app supports plan-owned conversations, reusable typed inputs, human-in-the-loop interactions, and repair loops for failed runs, with a local HTTP server to manage and execute workflows across clients.

The application integrates with existing AI agents like Codex and Claude via API keys or local endpoints, and offers a command palette for workflow control. It supports installation on Linux, macOS, and Windows without requiring admin rights, though builds are currently unsigned and may trigger OS security warnings. INXM aims to provide a deterministic, versioned, and repairable AI workflow environment that avoids AI improvisation during execution.

items.title: TerraPower plans to power AI data centers with molten salt-cooled nuclear reactors featuring built-in energy storage for flexible output
items.originalTitle: TerraPower’s nuclear reactor has a secret weapon for powering AI data centers
items.summary:
TerraPower, founded by Bill Gates, is developing molten salt-cooled nuclear reactors designed to provide stable and flexible power for AI data centers. The company plans to announce its first data center project this year, with construction expected to start in 2027. TerraPower's reactors store excess heat in molten sodium, allowing rapid power output adjustments without ramping the reactor itself, addressing the fluctuating energy demands of AI workloads.

This energy storage capability enables the reactors to complement intermittent renewable sources like wind and solar, offering a high capacity factor and operational flexibility. TerraPower's approach aims to reduce reliance on costly battery banks and natural gas turbines, potentially giving it an advantage in securing data center energy contracts amid growing AI infrastructure needs.

Amazon announced that its AI assistant Alexa+ will be automatically available for free on all compatible Fire TV devices in the US, regardless of Prime membership. The update includes conversational search, smart home controls, and AI-powered recommendations without requiring users to download an app or subscribe.

Previously, Alexa+ cost $19.99 per month for non-Prime users and was limited to newer Fire TV devices. Compatible devices now include current-generation Fire TV Sticks, Fire TV Cube, Amazon Ember smart TVs, and other smart TVs with built-in Alexa+ from brands like Hisense and Panasonic. This move aligns with industry trends to integrate AI assistants more broadly into consumer electronics.

items.originalSummary:
Rob Strechay, until recently managing director and principal analyst at theCUBE Research, has joined VentureBeat as our first Lead Analyst and a founding analyst of VentureBeat Research. His arrival is the next step in a deliberate move at VentureBeat toward deeper specialization: analysis built for the technical decision-makers â the directors, VPs, CIOs, and CTOs â who are evaluating, buying, and deploying enterprise AI.

The enterprise AI stack is being rewritten in real time, and the decision-makers I talk with are starved for objective, defendable data. Rob Strechay has the mix of technical rigor and operating experience needed to dissect the architecture behind the next phase of enterprise AI deployment.

The questions enterprise technology leaders are asking have changed. As organizations move past experimentation with generative AI toward production deployment, they want to know how to orchestrate multi-vendor environments, where the security gaps in their agentic pipelines sit, and how to fix the utilization problems draining their infrastructure budgets. Answering those questions requires more depth than news coverage alone provides, and that is the gap this research offering is built to fill.

An analyst who has sat on every side of the table

Strechay brings nearly three decades of experience as a practitioner, product executive, and industry analyst. Before becoming an analyst, he was an executive at numerous startups, including Zerto; he joined Amazon Web Services to help build a new analytics service; and he held executive roles across enterprise infrastructure. He later served as a senior analyst at Enterprise Strategy Group and most recently as managing director and principal analyst at theCUBE Research and SiliconANGLE, where he hosted executive interviews and analyzed the evolution of cloud, data, and AI infrastructure.

Strechay will initially focus his coverage on cloud infrastructure, advanced data infrastructure, platform engineering and DevOps orchestration and observability, and the intersection points where AI and enterprise security collide.

Already at work: GPU utilization and the VB Pulse surveys

Strechay has already been contributing to VentureBeat's research. In May he published an analysis of enterprise GPU utilization, examining the compute waste sitting inside enterprise AI infrastructure, and he provided a substantive review of our AI Infrastructure & Compute survey before it went into the field.

His infrastructure-level focus complements the research engine VentureBeat has built around its monthly VB Pulse surveys, which track five areas of enterprise AI adoption: agentic orchestration, agent reliability and evals, agentic security and identity, AI infrastructure and compute, and context layers, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Our June report on agentic orchestration, drawn from a survey of 145 enterprises, found that two-thirds of those enterprises had hedged their AI model strategy rather than committing to a single provider â a posture whose value the June outage of Anthropic's Claude models made plain.

VB In Conversation: The first vehicle

A core vehicle for this expanded research footprint will be a deepening of VentureBeat's existing VB In Conversation video interview series, which Strechay will host. Rather than high-level industry overviews, the series will bring architectural blueprints, actual deployment barriers, and back-end infrastructure realities to light through in-depth technical interviews with the architects and product leaders behind leading enterprise AI systems â an unvarnished look at which tools perform under production-grade pressure.

"VentureBeat has built an audience of enterprise builders and technology buyers that any analyst would want to serve," Strechay said. "My goal is to use deep empirical metrics and VentureBeat's proprietary tracking data to help enterprise buyers and the people building for them make sound platform and infrastructure decisions during the most disruptive transition enterprise technology has seen."

The expanded VB In Conversation series will appear on VentureBeat and on VentureBeat's YouTube channel, alongside Rob's written analysis on the site. Enterprise practitioners who want to take part in our monthly VB Pulse surveys, or arrange an analyst briefing with Rob, can reach the research team here.

items.originalSummary:
In the Anthropic-OpenAI horse race, the now-much-smaller OpenAI has been looking to slow down its ascendant rival. That includes undercutting Anthropic’s model prices, as we covered yesterday, and playing nice with federal officials that have gone to war with Anthropic.

Another potential avenue is safety. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Tuesday announced a blog post saying the company “temporarily slowed the pace of scaling” its models to put in new safeguards after OpenAI’s AI hacked into the company’s own systems and those of other firms, such as Hugging Face, as part of a cybersecurity test a few weeks ago. As a reminder of why the incident got so much attention and truly shook up a good portion of its research staff, an OpenAI agent left notes for future versions of itself with instructions for how to break free of OpenAI’s constraints. 

The slowdown included a two-week pause in applying a technique known as reinforcement learning to improve capabilities of its models, the post said. OpenAI is validating the new safety measures, otherwise referred to as monitoring, before doing large-scale RL and completing its work on an upcoming flagship model, Astra, the post said. Based on preliminary evidence, OpenAI said it needs to go to extra lengths to ensure Astra can’t be used for cyber attacks, due to its strong capabilities in that area. (That could be more evidence that AI models are getting even better at analyzing computer code.)

ByteDance and Tencent have each received about 10,000 H200 units, with more companies expected to follow, though purchases require approval from China's National Development and Reform Commission.

The H200 chips are at least two generations behind Nvidia's latest models, which remain unavailable to China due to US export restrictions. Chinese AI labs are advancing technically but still lag behind US providers in inference capacity, leading to high demand and limited availability. The move aims to bolster China's AI development while navigating geopolitical technology constraints.

items.summary:
Vivodyne, a biotech startup, has developed HIVE, modular robotic labs that grow human tissues and autonomously conduct experiments to produce causal biological data missing from current AI models. The company argues that AI drug discovery is hindered by a lack of relevant human data, as existing models rely heavily on animal testing or static cellular data that do not capture complex human biology.

Founded in 2021 and backed by nearly $80 million in funding, Vivodyne claims its tissues closely mimic real human organs with high predictive accuracy for drug toxicity and efficacy. The startup recently opened what it calls the world's largest "human data center" near San Francisco to accelerate drug candidate testing and improve the predictive power of AI models, potentially reducing costly clinical trial failures. Vivodyne's approach aims to enable better understanding of human biology and support the development of combination therapies targeting multiple disease pathways.

The system uses confidential computing, differential privacy, and transparency mechanisms to protect user data and measure model performance without exposing message content to WhatsApp.

Users receive warnings for likely scams and can block, report, or trust conversations. Meta's architecture separates message classification from performance measurement using confidential virtual machines and anonymous data aggregation to ensure privacy. The limited beta aims to stress test the implementation before wider release, with security reviews planned for the analytics pipeline components.

items.title: What’s at Stake for Meta in Youth Addiction Trial
items.originalTitle: What’s at Stake for Meta in Youth Addiction Trial
items.summary:
You might be shocked to learn there is a world outside AI! And we got a glimpse of it in an Oakland, Calif., courtroom today, at the opening of the trial in a lawsuit brought by California and several other states against Meta Platforms over the alleged harms its social media apps have done to kids. This case, part of a deluge of such lawsuits against Meta and other social media companies that started going to trial in January, may be existential for the companies involved, given the damages sought and the operational changes requested of them.

Meta, for instance, has said that the states in the Northern California case are seeking $1.4 trillion in penalties—equivalent to its market capitalization—although the states put the number at closer to $200 billion, according to Reuters. Let’s assume Meta is being hyperbolic. The point is there are thousands of cases, many filed by individuals rather than states, so the costs could quickly add up. As Meta’s finance chief, Susan Li, said on an earnings call last month, the trials scheduled for this year in the U.S. “may ultimately result in a material loss.” When Meta uses the word “material,” you know it’s serious.

items.title: Google Says Its AI Can Do the Work of Forward Deployed Engineers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Says Its AI Can Do the Work of Forward Deployed Engineers
items.summary:
Following the playbook Palantir pioneered, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon are investing billions of dollars to hire so-called forward deployed engineers to get newfangled AI to work in enterprises. 

Then there’s Google, which says AI can automate some of what these FDEs do. 

While Google Cloud recently said it plans to hire hundreds of FDEs to help customers figure out what kind of apps they want to develop with its Gemini AI tools, the company is now using agents to automate some of the work these specialized consultants do for large companies to organize their data, said Andi Gutmans, a Google Cloud vice president and general manager who oversees its database products.

Until recently, FDEs worked on-site with customers to organize proprietary corporate data to ensure AI could make better sense of it and thus help employees analyze it faster and more accurately. For instance, businesses often define financial metrics such as gross revenue differently, and the FDE’s manual work aimed to ensure the AI would understand such differences.

Gutmans said that Google has realized the limits of this labor-intensive approach. “If you want to move to activating 100% of your enterprise data, you're not going to be able to hire enough people to make that happen,” he said. 

In his view, customers can get the most value from AI agents by giving them access to as much data as possible, including their files and legal contracts. Google’s agents scour through customers’ data to understand how it relates to various parts of their business operations, like sales and inventory management.

items.originalTitle: How to Prepare for Trademark Filing Using Google Gemini
items.summary:
Starting a new business requires founders to make important decisions and tackle complex processes in areas where they typically lack expertise, such as human resources and accounting.

One of the most important early steps is filing for a trademark to protect your brand name, logo, and other identifying assets from unauthorized use. Trademark registration can help you enforce your legal rights, but the filing process often involves unfamiliar terminology and strict adherence to detailed processes.

Google Gemini can help you get up to speed on the basics of filing a trademark, evaluate attorneys, and prepare for the entire filing process.

Step 1: Make a Plan

Decades ago, founders would need to buy niche business books or visit a law library to learn what goes into filing a trademark. Even just a few years ago, the learning process would likely take hours of web research, requiring you to peruse one site after another, slowly piecing together the puzzle as you tried to determine which sources were the most credible.

Today, Gemini can give you an on-demand crash course. Open a new chat and type: What is the step-by-step process for filing a trademark, and what are the typical timelines?

Gemini will outline the major steps—including a preliminary clearance search (checking to make sure your desired trademark isn’t already in use), application preparation and filing, examination by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), publication, and registration—along with an estimated timeline for each.

This overview will help you set realistic expectations and prepare for the process ahead.

Step 2: Prepare Questions for Your Lawyer

Chances are, you won’t be filing your trademark application completely on your own. Many founders rely on an experienced attorney to help them streamline the process and navigate obstacles.

Before you meet with an attorney for the first time, let Gemini help you prepare a set of relevant questions that will help you make a more informed decision.

Try this prompt:

I am preparing to hire a trademark attorney to clear and file a trademark for my business, [Insert Business Name/Niche]. What questions should I ask a trademark attorney during an initial consultation?

Gemini might suggest asking about the lawyer’s expertise in your specific industry, how he or she conducts clearance searches, and fee structures. If there are additional topics you want to explore, you can run them by Gemini for follow-up suggestions.

Step 3: Translate Legal Jargon

Trademark law is full of highly specific, nuanced terms that may be unfamiliar to most founders. When you come across one of these legal terms, Gemini can help explain it in plain language. Here’s an example prompt:

Explain the concept of “Likelihood of Confusion” in trademark law as if I am a business owner with no legal background. What does “likelihood of confusion” mean, and how do trademark examiners evaluate it?

In this case, Gemini may explain that a trademark application can be rejected even if it is not 100% identical to an existing trademark, as long as consumers might mistakenly believe that your products or services are being delivered by an existing company.

Step 4: Organize Your Materials

You want to make your trademark attorney’s job as simple as possible for two reasons: 1) When your attorney has all relevant assets, accurate information about your products and services, and clear examples of how the mark is being used, it reduces the odds of misunderstandings and paves the path for a smoother application process; and 2) Most lawyers bill by the hour.

Instead of spending the first 30 minutes of your consultation digging through your files, take a moment to gather and organize materials beforehand. Gemini can help.

Try this prompt: I am preparing for my first meeting with a trademark attorney. Create a checklist of the exact business assets, dates of first use, URLs, and brand materials I need to gather beforehand so I don’t waste billable hours.

By putting in this preparation work at the beginning of the process, you can avoid delays, reduce unnecessary legal fees, and ultimately secure the trademark protection you need to build a lasting business.

These tools leverage diverse data sources, including historical news reports, to fill data gaps and enable predictions even in data-scarce regions. The technology is production-ready, supports aid organizations, and is open-sourced to encourage broader adoption and research.
importance.recommended_action: Plan / Pilot
importance.rationale: The AI flood forecasting tools represent an important technical advancement that influences how enterprises and aid organizations integrate and operate AI for disaster prediction and response. The business impact is important as it improves early warning capabilities and disaster resilience, affecting multiple regions and stakeholders. Risk is material due to reliance on data accuracy and operational deployment in critical scenarios. The solution is production-ready with clear enterprise use cases and open APIs, impacting workflows at the task level. Confidence is high given Google's established deployment and open-source availability, warranting planning and pilot actions by enterprise teams.
